lessons.title: Virtual Threads (Java 21)
lessons.html:
Project Loom - Virtual Threads

Millions of threads with minimal memory! Virtual threads make concurrency simple.

Traditional vs Virtual:

// Platform Thread (Heavy - 2MB stack)
Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("Heavy thread");
});
t.start();

// Virtual Thread (Lightweight)
Thread vThread = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
    System.out.println("Lightweight!");
});

Structured Concurrency:

try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    Future<Integer> result1 = scope.fork(() -> compute(1));
    Future<Integer> result2 = scope.fork(() -> compute(2));
    scope.join();
    scope.throwIfFailed();
}

  1. Modify the code example to handle edge cases
  2. Write a test case for the main functionality
  3. Refactor the code to improve performance or readability

Pattern Matching Revolution

Eliminates boilerplate instanceof + casting everywhere.

String result = switch (obj) {

    case String s when s.length() > 5 -> "long string";
    case null -> "null";

lessons.title: Record Patterns (Java 21)
lessons.html:
Record Patterns Deep Dive

Record patterns let you deconstruct records directly in pattern matching. This combines the power of records with pattern matching for extremely concise and readable code.

Basic Record Pattern:

record Point(int x, int y) {}
record Line(Point start, Point end) {}

static void printLineInfo(Object obj) {
    if (obj instanceof Line(Point(int x1, int y1), Point(int x2, int y2))) {
        System.out.println("Line from (" + x1 + "," + y1 + ") to (" + x2 + "," + y2 + ")");
    }
}

Nested Patterns:

if (obj instanceof Box(Container(Content c))) {
    System.out.println("Content: " + c);
}

switch (shape) {
    case Circle c when c.radius() > 10 -> System.out.println("Large circle");
    case Circle c -> System.out.println("Small circle");
    case Rectangle r -> System.out.println("Rectangle");
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Create a nested record structure for an AST and use pattern matching to evaluate expressions
  2. Implement a JSON parser using record patterns
  3. Compare the readability of record patterns vs traditional instanceof chains

Key Takeaways:

  • Record patterns work with any record type and support arbitrary nesting
  • Guards add conditional logic to pattern cases
  • The compiler verifies exhaustiveness for switch patterns

lessons.title: Structured Concurrency Patterns
lessons.html:
StructuredTaskScope Advanced

StructuredTaskScope provides a structured way to manage virtual threads, ensuring all tasks complete before the scope closes.

ShutdownOnFailure:

Response handle() throws ExecutionException, InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
        Future<String> user = scope.fork(() -> fetchUser());
        Future<Integer> orders = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrders());
        scope.join();
        scope.throwIfFailed();
        return new Response(user.resultNow(), orders.resultNow());
    }
}

ShutdownOnSuccess (Race):

String fastestResult() throws Exception {
    try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnSuccess<String>()) {
        scope.fork(() -> query("server1"));
        scope.fork(() -> query("server2"));
        scope.fork(() -> query("server3"));
        scope.join();
        return scope.result();
    }
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement a timeout pattern using structured concurrency
  2. Create a scatter/gather pattern collecting from multiple services
  3. Handle partial failures gracefully in a structured scope

Key Takeaways:

  • Structured concurrency prevents thread leaks
  • ShutdownOnFailure cancels all tasks on any failure
  • ShutdownOnSuccess is useful for redundant service calls

lessons.title: Advanced Streams & Custom Collectors
lessons.html:
Custom Collectors and Parallel Processing

Java Streams provide powerful data processing. Custom collectors enable complex aggregations.

Custom Collector:

Collector<Employee, ?, Map<String, Double>> avgSalaryByDept =
    Collector.of(
        HashMap::new,
        (map, emp) -> map.merge(emp.department(), emp.salary(), Double::sum),
        (m1, m2) -> { m1.putAll(m2); return m1; }
    );

Parallel Stream Pitfalls:

// Bad: shared mutable state
List<Integer> results = new ArrayList<>();
stream.parallel().forEach(results::add);  // NOT thread-safe!

// Good: use collect()
List<Integer> results = stream.parallel()
    .collect(ArrayList::new, ArrayList::add, ArrayList::addAll);

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement a collector that computes multiple statistics at once
  2. Create a parallel stream pipeline and benchmark against sequential
  3. Build a custom collector for paginated results

Key Takeaways:

  • Custom collectors encapsulate complex reduction logic
  • Parallel streams require thread-safe accumulation
  • Always benchmark before using parallel() in production

lessons.title: Foreign Function & Memory API
lessons.html:
FFM API - Project Panama

The Foreign Function & Memory API replaces JNI with pure Java bindings to native code.

Calling C Functions:

Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
MethodHandle printf = linker.downcallHandle(
    linker.defaultLookup().find("printf").get(),
    FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, ValueLayout.ADDRESS)
);
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment str = arena.allocateFrom("Hello from Java!\n");
    printf.invoke(str);
}

Memory Allocation:

try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment segment = arena.allocate(100);
    segment.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0, 42);
    segment.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, 8, 3.14);
    int i = segment.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0);
    double d = segment.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, 8);
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Write a Java program calling C's strlen via FFM
  2. Allocate native struct fields and read/write values
  3. Compare FFM vs JNI performance for matrix operations

Key Takeaways:

  • FFM provides type-safe native interop without JNI
  • Arena scopes manage native memory automatically
  • MethodHandle enables efficient native function calls

lessons.title: Virtual Threads - Pinning & Optimization
lessons.html:
Understanding Virtual Thread Pinning

Virtual threads can be pinned to carrier threads in synchronized blocks. Understanding pinning is crucial.

Pinning Scenarios:

// Pinning occurs in synchronized blocks
synchronized (lock) {
    Thread.sleep(1000);  // Carrier thread blocked!
}

// Solution: ReentrantLock
private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
void doWork() {
    lock.lock();
    try { Thread.sleep(1000); } // No pinning
    finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

ScopedValue:

private static final ScopedValue<User> CURRENT_USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handleRequest(User user) {
    ScopedValue.where(CURRENT_USER, user)
        .run(() -> processRequest());
}
void processRequest() {
    User user = CURRENT_USER.get();
    // No ThreadLocal overhead with virtual threads
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Profile a virtual thread app for pinning using JFR
  2. Refactor synchronized blocks to use ReentrantLock
  3. Implement ScopedValue for request context propagation

Key Takeaways:

  • Synchronized blocks pin virtual threads to carrier threads
  • ReentrantLock is the recommended replacement
  • ScopedValue is more efficient than ThreadLocal

lessons.title: Reactive Programming with Project Reactor

Mono and Flux Advanced Operators

Project Reactor provides reactive types for async data streams with backpressure.

Error Handling:

Flux<String> result = Flux.fromIterable(ids)
    .flatMap(id -> fetchFromService(id)
        .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just("fallback_" + id))
        .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofSeconds(1))
            .filter(IOException.class::isInstance)))
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30));

Combining Sources:

Mono.zip(getUser(id), getOrders(id), getReviews(id))
    .map(tuple -> new UserProfile(
        tuple.getT1(), tuple.getT2(), tuple.getT3()))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());

lessons.title: Observability & Production Readiness
lessons.html:
Metrics, Tracing, and Structured Logging

The three pillars of observability: metrics for trends, tracing for request flow, logging for debugging.

Micrometer Metrics:

@Service
public class MetricsService {
    private final Counter orderCounter;
    private final Timer orderTimer;

    public MetricsService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        orderCounter = Counter.builder("orders.created")
            .description("Total orders created").register(registry);
        orderTimer = Timer.builder("orders.processing.time")
            .description("Time to process order").register(registry);
    }

    public Order createOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        return orderTimer.record(() -> {
            Order order = orderRepository.save(convert(request));
            orderCounter.increment();
            return order;
        });
    }
}

OpenTelemetry Tracing:

@Configuration
public class TracingConfig {
    @Bean
    public OpenTelemetry openTelemetry() {
        return OpenTelemetrySdk.builder()
            .setTracerProvider(SdkTracerProvider.builder()
                .addSpanProcessor(BatchSpanProcessor.builder(
                    OtlpGrpcSpanExporter.builder()
                        .setEndpoint("http://otel-collector:4317").build())
                .build())
            .build().getOpenTelemetry();
    }
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Add custom metrics and visualize in Grafana
  2. Set up distributed tracing across 3 microservices
  3. Implement structured JSON logging with correlation IDs

Key Takeaways:

  • Metrics are aggregated over time (counters, histograms)
  • Tracing follows a single request across services
  • Structured logging enables automatic log parsing
